summary: Castroville bills itself as the "Artichoke Capital of the World," and the claim is not hyperbole — the cool, fog-laced coastal plain surrounding this one-square-mile town along Highway 1 produces a staggering share of California's commercial artichoke crop, and a giant artichoke-shaped roadside stand has greeted travelers here for decades. That agricultural backbone shapes nearly everything about daily life: the surrounding Salinas Valley flatlands offer wide-open farm horizons rather than ocean views, even though Monterey Bay sits only a few miles west, and the marine layer keeps average highs around 65°F year-round — pleasant for fieldwork, but sweater weather by most standards. At a median home value of roughly $649K against a median household income near $90K, the price-to-income ratio lands around 7.2, steep enough that buying requires substantial savings or dual incomes, while rents near $1,593 consume roughly 21% of that median — more manageable but still tight given a 14.6% poverty rate. The town is compact and walkable in the literal sense — just one square mile — yet it functions largely as a bedroom and agricultural-service community, with most professional employment requiring a drive into Salinas, Marina, or the Monterey Peninsula. Castroville is a place where coastal California's agricultural economy is the foreground, not the backdrop, and the tradeoff is living inside that economy's rhythms rather than beside them.
